title: Loop Filter Design
intro: The loop filter turns the pump's charge into the VCO control voltage and fixes the loop's bandwidth, phase margin and spur rejection. This page gives closed-form design equations for the second-order passive filter, the third-order extension and the active filter, with a worked example.

blocks.text: The second-order passive filter

blocks.alt: Three loop filters. (a) Second order: the pump current I_CP enters node V_cont, which has C_2 to ground and, in parallel, a resistor R in series with C_1 to ground. (b) Third order: the same plus a series resistor R_3 and a shunt capacitor C_3 whose node drives the VCO. (c) Active: an op-amp whose inverting input receives the pump current and is held at V_ref, with R in series with C_1 from output to inverting input and C_2 in parallel with that branch; the output is V_cont.
blocks.caption: Passive second- and third-order filters and an active filter.

blocks.text: The filter of the Charge-Pump PLLs page, $R$ in series with $C_1$ and $C_2$ in parallel, has transimpedance

blocks.tex: Z(s) = \frac{1 + sRC_1}{s\,(C_1 + C_2)\left(1 + sR\frac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\right)}, \qquad \omega_z = \frac{1}{RC_1}, \qquad \omega_p = \frac{C_1 + C_2}{RC_1C_2} = b\,\omega_z

blocks.text: with $b = 1 + C_1/C_2$. The open-loop gain of the PLL is $G(s) = \frac{I_P}{2\pi}Z(s)\frac{K_{VCO}}{Ns}$, so its phase is

The phase rises from $-180^\circ$, peaks at the geometric mean $\omega = \omega_z\sqrt{b}$, and falls back. Putting the crossover $\omega_c$ there gives the largest phase margin the capacitor ratio allows:

So $C_1/C_2 = 9$ ($b = 10$) gives 54.9°, $b = 13.9$ gives 60°, $b = 16$ gives 61.9° and $b = 20.4$ gives 65°. Razavi's rule of $C_2 \approx C_1/5$ to $C_1/10$ ($b$ = 6 to 11) corresponds to about 46° to 56°, if the crossover is placed optimally.
Design equations

Given $\omega_c$ and a phase margin, set $\sqrt{b} = \tan\mathrm{PM} + \sec\mathrm{PM}$, then place $\omega_z = \omega_c/\sqrt{b}$ and $\omega_p = \omega_c\sqrt{b}$. Requiring $|G(j\omega_c)| = 1$ gives the total capacitance; the zero and pole terms together contribute exactly $\sqrt{b}$ at $\omega_c$:

blocks.tex: C_1 + C_2 = \frac{I_PK_{VCO}}{2\pi N\,\omega_c^2}\sqrt{b}, \qquad C_2 = \frac{C_1 + C_2}{b}, \qquad R = \frac{\sqrt{b}}{\omega_cC_1}

blocks.text: These are exact for the continuous-time model. Banerjee's 'gamma optimisation' generalises them by letting the crossover sit off the phase peak (a factor $\gamma$), which trades a little phase margin for faster lock or less capacitance.

Raise the ratio and the phase bump becomes taller and wider; the label gives the margin at the designed crossover. Add a third pole at 3 times the crossover and see the margin fall by about 18°; at 10 times it costs under 6°.
Choosing the bandwidth

items: Noise: near the frequency where the VCO's free-running noise meets the in-band floor (In-Band Noise page). A noisy VCO wants a wide loop; a noisy reference or pump wants a narrow one.

Sampling limit: the continuous-time model holds only for $\omega_c$ well below $\omega_{ref}$. Gardner's analysis puts the stability limit near $\omega_{ref}/\pi$; designs keep $f_c$ at $f_{ref}/10$ to $f_{ref}/20$ or below.
Spurs and fractional-N noise: a narrower loop filters the reference spur and the sigma-delta quantization noise harder.
Settling: lock and channel-switching time scale roughly as a few to ten time constants of $1/(\zeta\omega_n)$, so faster settling needs a wider loop.

blocks.text: The third-order filter

A series $R_3$ and shunt $C_3$ after the second-order filter add a pole $\omega_3 = 1/(R_3C_3)$, about 20 dB per decade of extra attenuation at the reference. Keep $\omega_3$ at least 5 to 10 times $\omega_c$ (11° to 6° of margin lost) and $C_3$ small compared with $C_2$ (say below $C_2/2$) so it does not load the main filter; $R_3$ adds its own thermal noise, so keep it moderate. Fourth- and fifth-order filters follow the same pattern; above third order designers usually move to active filters or use simulation tools such as TI's PLLatinum Sim.
The active filter

An op-amp integrator with $R$ and $C_1$ in series in the feedback path (and $C_2$ across them) gives the same $Z(s)$ but holds the pump's output at $V_{ref}$. Advantages: the pump always sees the same voltage, so mismatch no longer varies with frequency; the VCO control range is that of the op-amp output, rail to rail or higher. Drawbacks: op-amp noise (its input-referred noise appears at the control line amplified by the impedance ratio), power, an extra pole from its finite bandwidth (keep its unity-gain frequency well above $\omega_c$), and a sign inversion.
Worked example
A 2.4 GHz integer-N loop: $f_{ref} = 40$ MHz ($N = 60$), $K_{VCO} = 2\pi\times200$ MHz/V, $I_P = 100\ \mu\text{A}$, $f_c = 400$ kHz ($f_{ref}/100$), phase margin 60°.

items: Zero at 107 kHz, pole at 1.49 MHz. A third pole at 4 MHz ($R_3 = 10$ kΩ, $C_3 = 4$ pF) adds 20 dB of attenuation at 40 MHz for 5.7° of margin.

Resistor noise: $\sqrt{4kTR} = 11.6$ nV/√Hz on the control line, which with $K_{VCO} = 2\pi\times200$ MHz/V is a frequency noise of 2.3 Hz/√Hz; check it against the VCO's own noise near the loop bandwidth.

blocks.title: Phase margin from a ratio
blocks.text: A design uses $C_1 = 100$ pF and $C_2 = 20$ pF. What is the best phase margin it can have, and where must the crossover be?
blocks.answer: 45.6 degrees, at 2.45 times the zero frequency.

blocks.title: Halving the bandwidth
blocks.text: In the worked example you halve the bandwidth to 200 kHz to reduce the reference spur. What happens to the capacitors and resistor?
solution: Total capacitance scales as $1/\omega_c^2$: four times larger, about 790 pF (or keep 197 pF and quarter $I_P$ to 25 µA, at a 6 dB noise penalty from the pump).
$R = \sqrt{b}/(\omega_cC_1)$: $\omega_c$ halves and $C_1$ quadruples, so $R$ halves to about 4.1 kΩ.
blocks.answer: Capacitors four times larger, resistor half as large.

blocks.title: Is the bandwidth too wide?
blocks.text: A PLL with a 20 MHz reference is designed with a 3 MHz loop bandwidth. Is the continuous-time design trustworthy?
solution: $f_c/f_{ref} = 0.15$, above the usual 1/10 limit and approaching the $1/\pi$ stability limit of the sampled loop.
The real phase margin will be lower than the continuous model predicts; reduce $f_c$ to 1 to 2 MHz or check with a discrete-time model.
blocks.answer: No: it is too close to the sampling limit.
